# The Great Biscuit Heist of Floor Four

Every office has a mystery. Ours had biscuits.

It began on a Monday, as these things do. Priya from accounts opened the shared tin at 10:14 and found it empty. Not half-empty. Not "someone took the last custard cream" empty. Scraped-clean, crumbs-swept, lid-put-back-politely empty. The tin had been full at 9:30. Forty-two biscuits had gone in forty-four minutes.

"That is nearly one a minute," said Tom, who had once been a maths teacher and never let anyone forget it.

By Wednesday it had happened three more times. A sign went up on the fridge: WHOEVER IS EATING THE BISCUITS, WE KNOW. Nobody knew. That was the problem.

So we did what any reasonable team would do. We set a trap.

Tom drew a floor plan on the whiteboard. Priya built a spreadsheet of who sat nearest the kitchen and who had "suspicious crumbs" on their keyboard. Marcus from IT pointed a webcam at the tin and named the recording "OPERATION DIGESTIVE". The tin was filled with exactly 50 biscuits, each one counted twice, and the lid was dusted with a thin layer of icing sugar for fingerprints.

At 9:58 on Thursday the camera caught a movement. A shape. Something low and fast.

It was not a colleague. It was Biscuit — the building manager's terrier, named, it turned out, for very good reasons. She had learned to nose open the kitchen door, climb the recycling bin, and lift the tin lid with her teeth. She ate twelve. The rest she carried, one at a time, to a nest under the stationery cupboard, where we later found 211 biscuits, three pens and a single sock.

The sign on the fridge now reads: BISCUIT, WE KNOW. The tin has a clip.

Tom says the numbers still don't add up. Nobody is asking him to explain.
